clue.text: Fell off boat in Devonshire (tweet circulated)

indicators.note: something circulated goes round and round, so its letters are spun into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boating accident off the Devon coast, with the news spreading on social media.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket makes the tweet look like an aside, but its letters join the county's fifteen-letter pool. Devonshire is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: To go over the side is a nautical phrase for dropping from a vessel's edge into the water.

clue.text: Older, but dreadfully worried

indicators.note: done dreadfully means done badly, so the letters come out mangled into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone getting on in years and fretting terribly about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreadfully worried' reads as one phrase, but 'dreadfully' belongs with the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Troubled and worried are direct synonyms for a mind full of anxiety and distress.

clue.text: Observe Ramadan ahead of time?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: go without food, as Muslims do in daylight hours during Ramadan
second meaning: describing a clock or watch that runs early

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests starting the holy month early; really the clue is two meanings, a verb of abstaining and an adjective for a clock that gains.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means abstain from eating; the adjective describes a timepiece showing a later hour than the true one.

clue.text: Aggressive lad had Nikes for running about

indicators.note: running about is moving all over the place, so the letters scatter into another order

parts.note: taken as written; Nikes are trainers made by the brand

explanation.surface: A tough youth who owned branded trainers to go jogging in.
explanation.walkthrough: Nikes are running shoes, so 'for running about' reads naturally as their purpose; it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A skinhead is a shaven-headed youth of a subculture associated with violence, so an aggressive young man.

clue.text: Notice gravy needs time to regulate

parts.note: an ad is a notice advertising something
jus is the thin gravy of meat juices on menus
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A cook's tip that gravy must be given time to settle.
explanation.walkthrough: Jus is the French culinary term for juice-based gravy, common on restaurant menus.
explanation.definitionFit: To regulate a mechanism is to tweak or set it correctly, which is to adjust it.

clue.text: What good fielder should do, covering every eventuality

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fielder in cricket or baseball ought to take every chance that comes
second meaning: an adjective for something comprehensive

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a playful reading of the hyphenated term as an instruction to a fielder; the second is its ordinary dictionary meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A catch-all clause or term is broad enough to include any situation not otherwise provided for.

clue.text: Offer to retain information for part of engine

indicators.note: to retain is to keep hold of, so one piece keeps another within it

parts.note: a bid is an offer, as at auction
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A bid to keep hold of the know-how about an engine component.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN, from 'general information', is informal British for the facts on something.
explanation.definitionFit: The big end is the larger end of a connecting rod, which grips the crankshaft in an internal-combustion engine.

clue.text: No letter is ever printed in this

definitions.text: No letter is ever printed in this

parts.words: No letter is ever printed in this
parts.note: surface reading: a medium where correspondence never goes to press, like private handwritten notes
setter's reading: printing means forming separate capitals by hand, which a cursive style never does since each character links to the next

explanation.walkthrough: 'Printed' suggests a press, but in handwriting it means separate unlinked characters, the opposite of cursive script.
explanation.definitionFit: Cursive handwriting connects each character to its neighbour, so none is formed in separate block style.

clue.text: Are strangely stressed and reserved

indicators.note: something done strangely is done oddly, so the letters come out in an unusual order

parts.note: taken as written
a stressed syllable is marked, as with an accent

explanation.surface: People who are oddly tense yet quiet and undemonstrative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserved' looks like a personality trait alongside 'stressed', but it means set aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Funds earmarked for a purpose are set aside for it, just as a table is reserved.

clue.text: Sort of acid, do you find me? Not at all

parts.note: asking 'do you find me so?' is asking 'am I?'
the flat reply of refusal

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they seem acidic and is told firmly they are not.
explanation.walkthrough: The question and reply read as one exchange: the question rephrased as 'Am I?', then answered 'No'.
explanation.definitionFit: Amino acids are the organic compounds that link together to build proteins.

clue.text: Relative settles in to new town …

indicators.note: to settle in somewhere is to take up residence inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: taken as written
an aunt is a relative
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A family member moving to a new town, with the ellipsis promising more of the story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New town' reads as a phrase, but 'new' gives a letter for the housing and the definition is the bare 'town'. Taunton is the county town of Somerset.
explanation.definitionFit: Taunton is a market town in south-west England, so it is one example of the category.

clue.text: … her husband has article needing a wash

parts.note: following on from the previous clue, an aunt's husband is an uncle
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Continuing the story: the aunt's spouse owns an item of clothing that must be laundered.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 11 Across, so 'her' is the relative there, and her husband is a familiar relation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unclean is dirty, so it is in need of washing.

clue.text: Heart ripped out of French town is horrible

indicators.note: tearing the heart out removes the central part, so the middle letter is lost

parts.note: ville is French for town

explanation.surface: A gruesome act of destruction in a French town, called horrible.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word for town has five letters, so its heart is the single third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Vile and horrible are synonyms for something extremely unpleasant or morally bad.

clue.text: Not using pen the right way?

definitions.text: Not using pen the right way?

parts.words: Not using pen the right way?
parts.note: surface reading: someone holding a pen incorrectly
setter's reading: 'right' is the side, so this is someone who writes with the other hand

explanation.walkthrough: 'The right way' suggests correctness; here it means the right hand, so the writer uses the opposite one.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who favours their sinister hand for writing does not hold the pen in their dextral one.

clue.text: Heart perhaps what will stop you playing any more

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a playing card in one of the two crimson suits

definitions.text: what will stop you playing any more
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the referee's sending-off signal in football

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks hearts as one example of the crimson suits; the second meaning is the football penalty that ends a player's match.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearts and diamonds are crimson suits in a deck, and a referee shows that colour to dismiss a player from the pitch.

clue.text: Greasy spoon turned up in cooked tart, one hand-made

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something up makes it read from bottom to top
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is placed within the other
cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a greasy spoon is a cheap British cafe serving fried food

explanation.surface: A diner where a home-made tart arrives with a spoon sticking up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: A greasy spoon is British slang for a cheap cafe; 'one hand-made' needs Britain's spelling with an E.
explanation.definitionFit: An artefact is an object made by human craft, especially one of historical interest, so something made by hand.

clue.text: Where choice food is brought back for pet to eat, all in a heap

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so it reads backwards
eating takes something inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: a pup is a young dog kept as a pet
a delicatessen sells fine foods

explanation.surface: Treats brought home for the dog, which gobbles everything piled in its bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening phrase is a definition-style description of a shop, and its letters run backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Things piled up are stacked in a heap, so the phrase means accumulated in a mound.

clue.text: Into the ground put a popular tropical crop

parts.note: to plant is to put into the ground
taken as written
in means fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: Advice to sow a fashionable tropical crop.
explanation.walkthrough: The first four words read as an inverted instruction; together they describe the verb for sowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Plantain is a starchy banana-like fruit grown widely in the tropics as a staple food.

clue.text: Conflict died, I dream

parts.note: d. is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies
taken as written
a vision is a dream or imagined picture

explanation.surface: A dreamer imagining that a war has ended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conflict died' reads as a war ending; 'Conflict' is the definition, and 'died' is its abbreviation in family trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Division means disagreement or discord between groups, a sense close to conflict.

clue.text: Make for senior teacher for such a direct confrontation

parts.note: to head to a place is to make for it
the head is the headteacher of a school

explanation.surface: Instructions to approach the headmaster for a face-to-face showdown.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the head is the principal of a school, the most senior teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A head-to-head is a contest or confrontation between two parties meeting face to face.

clue.text: Area to change, incorporating one large cage

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area

indicators.note: to incorporate something is to take it into the body of the whole, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: to vary is to change
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A plan to alter a space so it holds one big enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' looks like an anagram signal, but here it is the verb that supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviary is a large enclosure for keeping birds, big enough for them to fly inside.

clue.text: Getting changed a chore for old poet

indicators.note: something getting changed is being altered, so the letters take a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly writer finds dressing up a tiresome task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting changed' reads as dressing; it is the instruction to reorder the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace was a leading lyric poet of ancient Rome, author of the Odes, so a poet of antiquity.

clue.text: A most reduced state

indicators.note: something reduced is made shorter, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
most, as in 'most kind', means very

explanation.surface: A country in the worst possible condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a noun for a condition or a nation, but it is the verb meaning declare.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to assert or declare something firmly, which is to state it.

clue.text: Working dog, one with a cold perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a dog trained to detect drugs or explosives by scent
second meaning: someone who keeps snuffling through a blocked nose

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests one dog with a chill; the two halves are separate meanings, a detection dog and a person snuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Customs officers use trained scent-detection dogs, and a person with a head cold keeps drawing air noisily through the nose.

clue.text: There's the problem: I've lost all patience

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an exclamation on identifying exactly what is wrong
second meaning: an exasperated declaration that enough is enough

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are spoken exclamations, and one short phrase covers each: spotting the issue, and declaring one's tolerance exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said both when pinpointing a fault and when announcing that one will tolerate no more.

clue.text: A popular group, whichever way you look at it

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: if it looks the same from either direction, it reads identically forwards and backwards

parts.note: a famous band whose four-letter name is symmetrical

explanation.surface: An undeniably well-liked band, however you judge them.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds like a judgement on the group's popularity; it actually describes how the name reads in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: ABBA were the Swedish pop quartet behind Waterloo and Dancing Queen, hugely successful in the 1970s.

clue.text: An order from duke: cut off Yorick's extremities

indicators.note: cutting off removes parts, here the ends named next
extremities are the outermost parts, so the first and last letters are the ones to go

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for duke
the jester whose skull Hamlet holds

explanation.surface: A duke orders the beheading-style mutilation of Yorick, the jester from Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An order' sounds like a command from the duke, but it is a classical style of column.
explanation.definitionFit: Doric is one of the classical orders of architecture, with plain capitals on sturdy columns.

clue.text: From summit, all one can do is make concessions

definitions.text: From summit, all one can do is
definitions.meaning: first meaning: once at the top of a mountain, the only way is descent
second meaning: back down from a position in an argument

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a literal mountaineering truth, the second the figurative sense of retreating from a stance.
explanation.definitionFit: To climb down figuratively is to withdraw from a firm position and yield ground to opponents.
